title: Did Claude Help an Amateur Astronomer Discover a New Planet?
key_facts: Pavel Rabtsevich, a 28-year-old product manager in Spain with no formal astronomy training, searched public TESS space-telescope data using Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex.
By his account the data covered over 126,000 stars from November of last year to early January.
He found TIC 4206066, a star a little smaller than the Sun about 116 light-years away, whose brightness dips every 3.18 days; the dips also appear in 2018 and 2020 data.
He estimates a planet about 1.4 times Earth's size with a surface near 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit; a second dip every 11.13 days is weaker evidence.
He ran 74 tests with Claude Code trying to disprove his hypothesis.
His request for TESS to observe the star was approved; TESS will measure it every two minutes from 31 Oct to 26 Nov, and he has posted the predicted dimming times.
NASA Exoplanet Science Institute's Kevin Hardegree-Ullman says the main challenge is ruling out false positives such as binary stars, and AI will not necessarily help confirm planets.
quote_evidence: “If the star dims on time in November, this gets a lot more serious,” he wrote in an X post outlining his findings.

“The biggest challenge with confirming planets is that we have to rule out false-positive scenarios,” says Kevin Hardegree-Ullman, a research scientist at the NASA Exoplanet Science Institute (NExScI).

Rabtsevich is careful to emphasize that correlation does not necessarily equal causation: the pattern he detected in his AI-assisted investigation may turn out to be rooted in something other than an exoplanet.
why_it_matters_hint: A candidate planet found by an amateur with AI tools will be tested by TESS observations from 31 Oct 2026.
event_date: Rabtsevich's search was last month; he posted the findings this week (early Oct 2026)
notes: Candidate only; no outside review. Star count is Rabtsevich's own figure.
